item.title: ReplaySSM Restores Fast Decoding for State‑Space Layers in Hybrid LLMs
item.description:
ReplaySSM Restores Fast Decoding for State‑Space Layers in Hybrid LLMs

🔍 Overview

Hybrid large‑language models interleave state‑space model (SSM) layers with a few attention layers. Recent work – ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State – shows how to make those SSM layers fast again, removing a major latency bottleneck that appears at serving batch sizes.

🧩 How it works

ReplaySSM changes the way an SSM’s internal state is stored during generation:

  • The state is split into a checkpoint (a full copy of the SSM state) and a buffer of recent inputs.
  • Output computation reads only the buffer, while the checkpoint is updated lazily.
  • This separation eliminates three known problems:
    1. State traffic – the full state no longer moves every token.
    2. Rollback for speculative decoding – the buffer can be discarded without reverting a large state.
    3. Error accumulation in a quantized state – rounding errors no longer re‑enter the recurrence each step.

⚙️ Key details

  • Hybrid model examples – NVIDIA Nemotron 3, Qwen 3.5 through 3.8, Kimi‑K3, and GLM‑5.3‑Flash all use this pattern, with Mamba‑2, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) as the SSM layer.
  • Decoding bottleneck – at batch size 256 on a Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU, SSM layers dominate latency up to 100 K tokens of context (Figure 2, left). The model has five times as many SSM layers as attention layers.
  • State size comparison – one SSM layer’s FP32 state is 4 MiB per sequence, while an FP8 KV entry is 0.5 KiB per token. Thus an SSM state equals an attention KV cache for roughly 8 K tokens.
  • Speculative decoding – a drafter proposes T tokens, the target model verifies them, then rolls back to the last accepted token. Attention rolls back by moving a KV pointer; an SSM’s state has no cheap inverse, so engines store a full snapshot after each draft token. This costs one read and T writes per step and limits how many requests fit in GPU memory, making speculative decoding barely helpful for SSMs.
  • Quantization issue – the quantized state is both the output and the next update’s input, so rounding error recurs at every step.

🚀 Availability

  • The paper is on arXiv and the implementation is on GitHub.
  • ReplaySSM is integrated into NVIDIA TensorRT‑LLM, vLLM, and FlashInfer.
  • Production deployments include GLM‑5.3‑Flash and Kimi‑K3.

💡 Why it matters

By turning the SSM state into a cache of recent inputs rather than a constantly moved full tensor, ReplaySSM restores the speed advantages of attention‑only models for hybrid architectures. This enables existing speed‑up techniques—speculative decoding and low‑precision quantization—to be applied to models that heavily rely on SSM layers, broadening the practical utility of state‑space approaches in large‑scale inference.

📊 Model‑SSM mapping

Model SSM layer
NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Mamba‑2
Qwen 3.5 – 3.8 Mamba‑2, GDN, or KDA
Kimi‑K3 KDA
GLM‑5.3‑Flash Mamba‑2 / GDN / KDA

#ReplaySSM #SSM #HybridModels #InferenceOptimization

Source: ReplaySSM: Rethinking State Storage for Faster Hybrid-Model Decoding | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Topograph Open Source Toolkit for Topology-Aware GPU Scheduling
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Topograph Open Source Toolkit for Topology-Aware GPU Scheduling

NVIDIA has introduced Topograph, an open source toolkit designed to identify cluster network topology to enable workload managers to make topology-aware scheduling decisions.

💡 Why it matters

AI factories are power-limited systems that require full optimization to deliver maximum value. Because GPUs exchange data continuously during training and inference, distributed workloads benefit from communication locality. Poor workload placement can lead to:

  • Fragmented topology domains
  • Increased traffic across shared links
  • Reduced throughput and higher job costs
  • GPUs consuming provisioned power while waiting for data without advancing the workload

Topograph prevents these bottlenecks by mapping how cluster hardware is connected, allowing schedulers to favor nearby resources and avoid spreading tightly coupled workloads across distant domains.

🧩 How it works

Topograph solves the problem of maintaining an accurate view of GPU and fabric relationships as a cluster changes. It uses two primary concepts:

  • Providers: These discover topology from cloud APIs or on-premises systems and normalize it into a canonical model.
  • Engines: These translate the normalized model into formats expected by various workload managers.

Within the NVIDIA DSX OS cluster orchestration layer, Topograph works alongside KAI Scheduler and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to enable topology-aware gang scheduling.

⚙️ Key details

Topograph supports a variety of hardware and software integrations to ensure the scheduler works from current data rather than a manually maintained snapshot.

Component Supported Integration/Requirement
Cloud Providers Google Cloud, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, and OCI
On-Premises Providers InfiniBand (with ibnetdiscover), NetQ (for Spectrum-X or Multi-Node NVLink domains)
Engines/Outputs Kubernetes node labels, Slurm topology configuration, Slinky ConfigMaps, Node Feature Discovery (NFD) resources, instance-oriented topology JSON
Slurm Engine Requires a writable volume for its configured topology.conf output path
NFD Engine Requires the alpha NodeFeatureGroupAPI feature gate
Crusoe Provider Runs in Kubernetes; reads fabric and accelerator-domain labels from Crusoe Managed Kubernetes nodes

🚀 Availability

Topograph is an open source toolkit with an open provider interface, allowing operators to add and contribute providers for their own environments upstream. As of September 16, 2026, the toolkit supports various provider-to-engine output combinations, though requirements may vary by version and configuration.

#NVIDIA #GPU #Kubernetes #Slurm #AIInfrastructure

Source: Topology-Aware Workload Scheduling with NVIDIA Topograph | NVIDIA Technical Blog
